title: Probability
summary: Find probabilities of compound events using lists, two-way tables and tree diagrams, use the rules for mutually exclusive, complementary and independent events, and compare predictions with relative frequencies.

items: When outcomes are equally likely: $P(E) = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$.
Relative frequency $= \dfrac{\text{number of times the event occurred}}{\text{number of trials}}$; it approaches $P(E)$ as the number of trials grows.

notes.text: A **compound event** involves two or more things happening, such as tossing two coins. A **tree diagram** shows every outcome: each stage branches out, and the probability is written on each branch.

notes.caption: Tree diagram for tossing a coin twice. Multiply along the branches: each outcome has probability ½ × ½ = ¼.

notes.title: Worked example 1
notes.problem: Two coins are tossed. Find (a) $P(\text{exactly one head})$ and (b) $P(\text{at least one head})$.
steps: (b) At least one head: everything except $TT$, so $1 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: "At least one" problems are often easiest using the complement: $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})$.
When two dice are rolled, a two-way table shows all $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely outcomes. Here each cell shows the **sum** of the two dice.

notes.title: Worked example 2
notes.problem: Two dice are rolled. Find (a) $P(\text{sum} = 8)$, (b) $P(\text{sum} > 9)$, (c) $P(\text{a double})$.
steps: (c) Doubles lie on the diagonal: $(1;1), (2;2), \ldots, (6;6)$, which is 6 outcomes. $P = \frac{1}{6}$.

notes.text: Two-way tables are also used to organise survey data. Probabilities are then found by reading the right cell and dividing by the correct total.

Events that **cannot happen at the same time**, such as rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 with one die. For mutually exclusive events, $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$. So $P(2 \text{ or } 5) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.

Events where the outcome of one **does not affect** the other, such as tossing a coin and rolling a die. For independent events, $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$. So $P(\text{head and } 6) = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: A coin has no memory. After three heads in a row, the probability of a tail on the next toss is still $\frac{1}{2}$. Each toss is independent.

To predict how often an event will happen, multiply its probability by the number of trials: in 120 rolls of a die you expect about $\frac{1}{6} \times 120 = 20$ sixes. The actual result will usually be close to, but not exactly, the prediction.

notes.title: Worked example 3
notes.problem: A spinner has 4 equal sections, one of them blue. It is spun 200 times and lands on blue 62 times. Compare the relative frequency with the probability.
steps: The result is higher than expected. This may be chance, or the spinner may be unfair; many more spins would be needed to decide.

items: Use lists, tree diagrams or two-way tables to find all outcomes of compound events.
Tree diagrams: multiply along the branches; add the probabilities of the outcomes you want.
Mutually exclusive: $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$. Independent: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$.
Expected number = probability × number of trials.

questions.prompt:
In a class of 40, each learner plays one sport. 18 boys play soccer, 4 boys play netball, 6 girls play soccer and 12 girls play netball. A learner is chosen at random.
(a) Draw a two-way table.  (1)
(b) Find $P(\text{girl})$, $P(\text{boy who plays netball})$ and $P(\text{soccer})$.  (3)
questions.memo:
(a) Rows boys/girls, columns soccer/netball, with totals 22 boys, 18 girls, 24 soccer, 16 netball ✓ (1)
(b) $P(\text{girl}) = \frac{18}{40} = \frac{9}{20}$ ✓
$P(\text{boy and netball}) = \frac{4}{40} = \frac{1}{10}$ ✓
$P(\text{soccer}) = \frac{24}{40} = \frac{3}{5}$ ✓ (3)

questions.memo:
(a) $\frac{62}{200} = 0{,}31$ ✓ (1)
(b) $\frac{1}{4} \times 200 = 50$ ✓ (1)
